p.x:
Everyone in my family has a different hobby. My dad loves fishing. Every Sunday, he goes to the river with his friends. My mum makes beautiful model houses from paper and wood.
My little brother likes playing cards and doing puzzles. He's only seven, but he's very good at them! My grandmother can knit and sew; last winter she made me a red scarf.
My hobby is chess. I'm in the chess club at school, and we meet every Wednesday. When we play, we take turns, and you have to think carefully before you move. I'm not an expert yet, but I'm getting better. Next month, I'm going to play in my first competition!

Ten years ago, many people thought board games were old-fashioned. Video games on phones and consoles seemed much more exciting. But today, board games are popular again, especially among young adults.
In many cities, there are now board game cafés, where you can pay a small fee and play hundreds of different games. Some games are simple: you roll the dice and move around the board. Others are more of a challenge and can take hours to finish.
Why are they so popular? One reason is that people want to spend leisure time with friends without looking at a screen. Board games are relaxing and sociable, and even competitive players can have fun. Beginners can usually learn the rules in a few minutes.
Of course, video games are still very popular. Many gamers enjoy reaching a higher level or unlocking new characters. Other people prefer quieter hobbies, such as stamp collecting, camping, hiking, origami, a jigsaw or a crossword. As one café owner says, "There's a game for everyone."

Not long ago, a teenager who spent hours on video games was considered to be wasting time. Today, the best players compete in esports tournaments watched by millions, and top professionals earn salaries comparable to those of traditional athletes. Gaming has become one of the world's largest entertainment industries.
This transformation raises interesting questions about the nature of hobbies. Psychologists have long argued that leisure activities are not merely ways to pass time but are essential to wellbeing. Activities that require concentration, such as knitting or building models, can be deeply therapeutic, reducing anxiety by focusing the mind on a single task. Learning to master a difficult skill also brings a sense of achievement that many people do not find in their work.
Modern games offer similar benefits. Immersive virtual worlds allow players to create an avatar, solve complex problems and cooperate with others in multiplayer adventures. Some research suggests that certain games can improve reaction times and spatial awareness, which is why some pilots train with a joystick-based simulator.
However, experts warn that the line between enthusiast and addict can be thin. Games designed to reward players constantly can make it hard to stop, and some people become obsessed, gaming through the night or binging for entire weekends. As with any pastime, the key appears to be balance: hobbies should enrich life, not replace it.
